title: SRE Standards: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Runbooks and Incident Reviews
author: Michael Chen
body:
Summary
-------
This document defines Redwood Inference SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning for inference and control-plane services, reliability initiatives and improvement processes, incident review expectations, operational tooling, and canonical runbook templates. The goal is to provide a single, actionable reference for on-call engineers, service owners, and platform teams.

Scope
- Applies to all public and internal services owned by engineering teams, with emphasis on inference endpoints, routing, and the control plane (accounting, billing, and routing).
- Excludes non-production experimental services unless they are used by customers or carry a business SLA.

SLOs and Error Budgets
---------------------
Principles
- Measure user-facing impact where possible. SLOs should represent user-visible outcomes (availability, latency, correctness).
- Keep SLOs simple and action-oriented. Prefer a small number (1-3) of SLOs per service.
- Error budgets are the operational contract: they enable controlled risk (launches, rollouts) and guide automatic mitigation.

Mandatory metadata for every SLO
1. SLI definition (how it is measured).
2. SLO target (numeric).
3. Measurement window (rolling 30d recommended; 90d for long-lived services).
4. Owner and alerting destinations (team and PagerDuty service).
5. Error budget burn policy (thresholds and actions).

SLO examples
| service                        | SLI                                 | SLO target        | window | alert threshold (burn rate) | pagerduty | owner-team |
|-------------------------------|-------------------------------------|-------------------|--------|-----------------------------|-----------|------------|
| inference-api (public)        | successful responses (HTTP 2xx)     | 99.95% availability | 30d   | 14-day burn rate > 1.5x     | PAGER-API | serving-team |
| inference-api (latency p95)   | p95 response time (in ms)           | <= 300 ms         | 30d   | sustained p95 > 400 ms (72h) | PAGER-API | serving-team |
| embedding-service             | successful embeddings (200)         | 99.9%             | 30d   | 7-day burn rate > 2x        | PAGER-EMB | embeddings-team |
| control-plane (billing writes)| write success to ledger             | 99.99%            | 90d   | any 24h outage              | PAGER-CTRL| platform-team |

Error budget policy (standard)
- Green: remaining error budget >= 50%: normal operations, safe to proceed with low-risk rollouts.
- Yellow: 20% <= remaining < 50%: throttle high-risk changes, increase monitoring cadence, communicate to stakeholders.
- Red: remaining < 20%: freeze risky rollouts, prioritize remediation; require SRE approval for any change.
- Critical burn (overnight burn rate > 4x or 24h continuous degradation): follow Sev1 playbook and consider customer-facing communications.

Automated responses tied to burn thresholds
- When 50% used: create internal incident-triage ticket, auto-escalate to SRE lead.
- When 80% used: apply routing fallbacks if applicable (route to warm model pool / degrade to lower-capacity availability mode).
- When 95% used: block all non-hotfix deploys to the owning service until error budget is recovered.

Capacity Planning
-----------------
Objectives
- Ensure sufficient headroom to meet SLOs during regular usage and expected bursts.
- Track capacity for both CPU/GPU inference pools and control-plane services separately.
- Maintain an evidence-backed plan for capacity purchases (Dedicated offerings) and autoscale behavior.

Key metrics to track (minimum)
- Sustained RPS (requests per second) over 24h, 7d, and 30d windows.
- Tail latency (p95, p99) and successful token throughput for model-serving paths.
- Average and 95th CPU/GPU utilization per instance class.
- Request queuing time and queue length at ingress (ms and count).
- Cold-start rate for model instances and cache hit ratio for KV/prefix cache.

Capacity targets and headroom
- Target steady-state utilization: 60% avg, 75% p95 for inference GPU pools. This protects against workload spikes and kernel-runtime variance.
- Burst buffer: maintain 20% spare capacity above projected 95th percentile demand for customer-facing hosted API.
- Warm pool sizing: maintain warm/model-ready capacity to cover the median burst size (measured as 5-minute peak over baseline).

Sizing rules (example)
1. Collect baseline: 30-day peak RPS = P. Expected 6-month growth = g (percent).
2. Required capacity = (P * (1 + g)) / per-instance-throughput.
3. Add headroom = Required capacity * 1.20 (20% buffer).
4. Reserve capacity for failover (N+1): add capacity equivalent to one instance class or 10% whichever is larger.

Capacity table (example classes)
| instance_class | per-instance throughput (rps) | target_utilization | min_reserve | notes |
|----------------|-------------------------------:|-------------------:|------------:|-------|
| gpu-large (A)  | 120                           | 60%                | 1 instance  | general-purpose transformer models |
| gpu-xlarge (B) | 220                           | 60%                | 1 instance  | larger models / batching heavy |
| cpu-medium     | 80                            | 70%                | 2 instances | control-plane and preproc |

Autoscaling and throttles
- Prefer conservative autoscaling with predictive warm pools for model-serving. Autoscalers should scale on combined signals: queued requests, p95 latency, and GPU utilization.
- Add max-surge constraints in Dedicated deployments to avoid noisy neighbor effects.
- Implement per-tenant/request throttles for free-tier customers to protect paid capacity.

Reliability Initiatives
-----------------------
Program structure
- Quarterly reliability goals (OKRs) for platform and product teams. Examples: reduce p99 tail latency by 25% for inference-api; reduce cold-start rate by 50%.
- Postmortem-driven improvements: prioritize fixes with estimated Mean Time To Restore (MTTR) benefit and low rollout risk.
- Red-team / game-days: simulate capacity loss and region failover at least twice per quarter for critical services.

Standard reliability initiatives
- Continuous batching and caching audit: ensure prefix/KV cache hit rates are within target range (>= 85%).
- Model-variant fallbacks: maintain at least one lower-cost compatible model per cataloged heavy workload to enable graceful degradation.
- Kernel-level performance regression tests in CI: any PR that changes runtime must include benchmark artifacts and performance gating.

Incident Review Standards
------------------------
Severity definitions
- Sev1: Customer-facing outage impacting >10% of requests or inability to serve tokens for >15 minutes.
- Sev2: Significant degradation (increased tail latency or errors) impacting multiple customers but mitigated partially.
- Sev3: Localized issues affecting small customer subset or internal tooling.
- Sev4: Informational, no immediate customer impact.

Incident lifecycle requirements
1. Declare severity within 15 minutes of recognizing user impact.
2. Create an incident record (issue tracker ticket) with timeline, primary owner, and initial mitigation steps.
3. Post initial internal incident update within 30 minutes.
4. If Sev1/Sev2 and customer-facing, publish public status updates every 60 minutes until mitigation.
5. Triage and assign postmortem within 3 business days.
6. Postmortem publish and action-item list within 14 days.

Postmortem template (required fields)
- Title, incident id, date/time window, severity.
- Impact summary (customers affected, estimated requests lost).
- Timeline with timestamps (ISO8601).
- Root cause analysis (technical and organizational contributing factors).
- Remediation and mitigation steps taken during the incident.
- Action items (owner, due date, type: mitigating, preventative).
- Follow-up verification plan and metric(s) to confirm fix.
- Link to dashboards, logs (retention pointers), and runbook references.

Blamelessness and learning
- Postmortems must be blameless and focus on system changes and process improvements. Personal attribution is not included in the public postmortem.

Operational Tooling
-------------------
Required stack (canonical)
- Metrics: Prometheus + Cortex remote write; metric types: counters, gauges, histograms for latency.
- Tracing: Jaeger (or Honeycomb where high-cardinality tracing is required).
- Logs: Loki for short-term troubleshooting; archived logs to S3 with lifecycle.
- Dashboards: Grafana with per-service folders and standardized dashboard templates (availability, latency, capacity).
- Alerting: Alertmanager -> PagerDuty; all alerts must have runbook links and noise suppression (dedup / grouping).
- Incident tooling: Statuspage (public) + internal incident board (Jira + Confluence incident page template).
- CI/Bench: runtime-bench (internal CI job) for kernel/runtime perf regressions.

Observability standards
- Instrument SLIs at the ingress and at key service boundaries (router -> model pool -> KV cache -> response).
- Use consistent labels: service, route, model_variant, region, instance_class, customer_tier.
- Metric cardinality: avoid unbounded label cardinality (limit customer_id to a sampled dimension).

Runbooks (canonical templates)
----------------------------
Every runbook must include:
- Title and scope.
- Symptoms (what to look for in dashboards and logs).
- Impact assessment (how to estimate customer impact).
- Immediate mitigation steps ( numbered, executable ).
- Root-cause investigation steps and useful queries.
- Rollback and recovery procedures.
- Post-incident verification steps.
- Known limitations and related runbooks.

Runbook: High error rate on inference-api (example)
1. Confirm alert: open Grafana dashboard 'inference-api / availability'. Check 5m and 1h panels for errors.
2. Check SLO and error budget: open SLO dashboard and check remaining budget.
3. Determine scope: run queries (Prometheus) to identify errors by route and model_variant.
   - promql (example):
     rate(http_requests_total{service="inference-api",status!~"2.."}[5m])
4. If errors concentrated on single model_variant: temporarily route to fallback variant using routing API:
   - curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' "https://control-plane.internal/api/v1/route-override" -d '{"route":"/v1/generate","model_variant":"fallback-small"}'
5. If errors are widespread and due to backend overload: increase warm-pool for model variant, or scale GPU pool:
   - kubectl scale deployment model-pool-variant-a --replicas=10 -n inference
6. If control-plane writes are failing: check database (primary) availability and apply standard DB failover runbook.
7. If mitigation requires code rollback: follow release rollback checklist (see related page).
8. Add annotation to incident ticket with root-cause candidate and attach logs (last 30 minutes).

Quick verification commands
- Check pods: kubectl get pods -n inference -o wide --selector=app=inference-api
- Tail logs: kubectl logs -f deployment/inference-api -n inference --since=10m
- Check queue length: curl -s "https://observability.internal/api/queues?service=inference-api" | jq

On-call and Escalation
----------------------
- PagerDuty is the canonical escalation. Each service must be mapped to a PagerDuty escalation policy.
- On-call roster: primary (30m response), secondary (2h), SRE lead (4h).
- For Sev1, the primary must acknowledge within 5 minutes and start triage within 15 minutes.

Change control during burn
- During Yellow/Red error budget states, require SRE approval for deploys to affected services. SREs log approval in the deployment ticket with timestamp and rationale.

Template: Runbook Ownership and Review
- Owner: team that operates the service (must be an SRE or engineer on the roster).
- Review cadence: runbooks reviewed quarterly; critical service runbooks reviewed monthly.
- Testing: runbooks must be exercised in a game-day at least once per quarter.

Appendix: Example alerts and thresholds
- inference-api-availability-critical: if availability < 99.9% over 30m -> P0
- inference-api-latency-p95-warning: p95 > 350 ms for 15m -> P1
- model-pool-queue-length: queue_length > 100 for 5m -> P1
